description: Barriers, cost of capital and cross listing. As depicted in red, Cluster 1 is the largest cluster of the network (see Figure 8). The documents of this cluster mainly concern the barriers in international listing and how cross listing overcomes these barriers and reduces the cost of capital of cross-listed securities. Multiple barriers in cross-listing include low credit ratings, high and volatile inflation, exchange rate regulations and an inadequate regulatory and accounting environment (Bekaert, 1995). Errunza and Miller (2000) disclosed that high taxation and transaction costs, restrictions on foreign ownership, and foreign exchange transactions limit the free flow of capital from the domestic market to the global market. Studies in this cluster provide that as the financial markets have become more globalised, more companies are opting to cross list their stock on exchanges outside their home country. Geographical, economic, cultural and industrial proximity seems to be the most relevant factor in selecting an overseas listing venue (Sarkissian and Schill, 2004). Domowitz et al. (1998) assert that corporate governance issues influence firms’ decisions to cross list their securities. Listed firms’ securities in the international market have less cost of capital (Miller, 1999. Reese and Weisbach, 2002). Further, Karolyi’s (2006) research work challenges the conventional wisdom that firms opt for cross-listed securities because it serves the benefit of reducing capital. his work provided other evidence which motivates overseas listings.

Corporate governance and cross-listing. This cluster (green colour) represents better corporate governance through cross-listing constraints on the private benefit activities of controlling shareholders. Improving the corporate governance system through cross-listing is known as the “bonding hypothesis” (Bell et al., 2012). In most countries, the weak local legally protected environment provides poor protection to minority shareholders and gives less importance to minorities. controlling shareholders can easily extract personal benefits from the firms they control (Doidge, 2004). For greater investor protection, foreign firms listed on USA exchanges “bond” themselves to the USA regulatory regime (Bellet al., 2012). Scholars in this cluster have contributed to the corporate governance literature by arguing that decision to cross list in the US exchange can reduce the agency problems (Bell et al., 2012. Doidge, 2004. Doidge et al., 2009b), improve disclosure practices (Doidge, 2004. Siegel, 2005. Eleswarapu and Venkataraman, 2006) and restrict the activities of controlling shareholders by providing addition scrutiny from various capital market intermediaries (Bell et al., 2012. Doidge et al., 2004, 2009b). Moreover, Siegel (2005) states that in case of ineffective US law enforcement, “reputational bonding” explains the growth of cross listings better than “legal bonding”. Ferreira and Matos (2008) emphasise that institutional investors seek to invest in the stock of large companies and companies with excellent governance indicators, while foreign institutional investors prefer to invest in US cross-listing exchange firms.

Disclosure and cross listing. The third cluster depicts blue colour bubbles. The central theme of this cluster primarily focussed on the disclosure of information standards when firms opt to cross list. Firms listed in the USA must comply with information disclosure standards and requirements that reduces information asymmetry and minimises the cost of capital (Bailey et al., 2006. Iatridis, 2013). With a sample of 192 companies from Australia, Canada and the USA, Robb et al. (2001) reveal that internationally-oriented and larger firms are the main disclosers of non-financial information. Moreover, Seetharaman et al. (2002) state that auditors also charged higher fees from cross-listed firms to offset the risk of litigation. Nevertheless, the cross listing in US exchange is positively related to compliance with International Accounting Standards (IAS) and the United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (US GAAP) (Glaum and Street, 2003). Few scholars in this cluster discussed the models of earning (Easton, 2004) and earnings management in crosslisting firms (Lang et al., 2003, 2006. Pincus et al., 2007). Lang et al. (2003) conclude that crosslisting firms are less involved in earning management. Further, Lang et al. (2006) document that firms reconciling to US GAAP has more evidence of earnings management than firms that prepare their local accounts according to US GAAP. Also, both companies have more significant evidence of earnings management than the US companies.

Investors’ decisions, trading activities and cross listing. Studies in this cluster (yellow) mainly focus on investors’ decisions and trading activities in domestic firms affected by firms’ internationalisation. Firms listed on the USA stock exchange adhere to the disclosure practices and reporting requirements that reduce the information asymmetry in USA stock (Jiang and Kim, 2005). Aggarwal et al. (2007) highlight different factors that motivate investors to choose ADRs rather than the underlying shares of US-listed international firms. They propound that investors who own ADRs have better legal protection that encourages them to buy ADRs, especially in a low-protection environment. Bae et al. (2006) highlight that openness events such as official liberalisation, cross listing of shares overseas or listing a closed-end country fund increase the availability of information in emerging stock markets. Halling et al. (2008), Kalev et al. (2008) and Levine and Schmukler (2006, 2007) discuss the impact of cross listing on the trading activities of native firms. Levine and Schmukler (2006, 2007) argue that the internationalisation of firms has a detrimental impact on the trading activity of local firms as the trading of international businesses shifts from home to international markets, and this mobility, along with the decline in national trading of international firms, has adverse ripple effects on the trading activity of domestic firms. Moreover, Halling et al. (2008) show the domestic turnover rate in both emerging and developed economies. They claim that cross listing in developed corporations raises the local turnover rate, whereas it does not in emerging markets.
